draft.title: Drawing charts and graphs
card: Column graph
Use it to compare separate groups, such as the number of students in each year level. Draw gaps between the columns.
Line graph
Use it to show how something changes over time, such as a temperature each month. Join the points with a line.
Pie chart
Use it to show how parts make up a whole. Each slice is a share of 360°. Example: 1/4 of the whole is 1/4 × 360° = 90°.
Every graph needs a title, labels on both axes and an even scale, such as 0, 10, 20, 30. A table is a good choice when exact values matter.
draft.remember: Match the graph to the data, then add a title, labels and an even scale.

a.q: Which graph best shows a town's rainfall each month over one year?
opts: A column graph with no labels
a.why: Rainfall each month is a change over time, so a line graph suits it. A pie chart shows parts of a whole, and the rainfall figures are not shares of a total that matter here.

b.q: In a survey of 40 students, 10 chose bus to get to school. What angle is the bus slice on a pie chart?
b.why: The bus share is 10/40 = 1/4, and 1/4 × 360° = 90°. The answer 144° comes from 40 ÷ 10 mixed up with 360 × 0.4, so it does not match the share of students who chose bus.
b.clue: Find the fraction of the whole, then take that share of 360°.

problems.detail: 'Every graph needs a title, labels on both axes and an even scale' is placed straight after the pie chart, but a pie chart has no axes or scale. Say this applies to column and line graphs, and that a pie chart needs a title and labelled slices.
The why's account of 144° ('40 ÷ 10 mixed up with 360 × 0.4') is muddled and could confuse students. 144° is 0.4 × 360°, which comes from wrongly using 40% instead of 10/40 = 25%.

check.summary: Both questions have a clear correct answer (line graph; 90°). The card wrongly implies a pie chart needs labels on both axes, and the why for (b) explains the 144° distractor in a confusing way.
